utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Mr. Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-01-48-T, the Prosecutor versus Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Before having the witness, I believe Mr. Morrissey has something to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I have, Your Honour. Your Honours I've just got a concern to raise about the way this cross-examination is proposed to proceed and I want to protest against an attempt that is made to use the statement of a person who was not a witness, was not on their witness list even before the withdrawing of many witnesses, and that it should be done in the way that it's proposed. Now, there are three reasons why we say that it's improper to use this and shouldn't be permitted to use this statement in the way that the Prosecutor wants to. The first one is that that statement itself is very unreliable. We have spoken to that individual person, and I'm in a position to call evidence about what she called us and the investigator Medina Delalic is in court and I can call letter now if needs be to prove what it is that that particular person, Ms. Dzogic said to the Defence. But in brief, what occurred was that she was visited by us, by the Defence team, in Zenica in June of this year and she offered, among other things to help us to finds the telephone number of the current witness. In the end it was somebody else who provided it but she made that offer. In the end we contacted the current witness. Your Honour, perhaps we should move into the private session for the purposes of this part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We will go to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, if there is any legitimate forensic purpose for showing this witness that crime-scene video, I'm not going to object to it. But it appears to me there can be none because he didn't see it and didn't go to the village. So it seems to me that it's more by way of making a statement to the Court rather than helping the witness in any way. But if there be any other -- and it's also important to realise that we are not calling this witness to prove anything about the crime scene but just to prove what he knew at the time. So that's why we would object to that being done unless there be shown some clear reason why it should be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Re? Do you have any reply?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, I'm in the middle of my cross-examination. This is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: On the second part.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In our submission, that's ambush. That's trying to prevent the Prosecution putting its case, if it needs to. If I wish to show the video to -- or a portion of the video to the witness, if it becomes necessary, based upon the conclusions he has drawn from his interviews or statements with all the people, and the conclusions he has given before the Court as to what he thinks happened in Uzdol, I'm entitled to confront the witness with contrary evidence if it comes to that. Now it's not for my learned friend at this point and it was to point out to the Court what I should or shouldn't be doing in cross-examination. We never once did that with them and we wouldn't presuppose to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe that Mr. Morrissey just reminded us about the documents you are going to use, which should be relevant to this case. I understand that there is a dispute between the parties how those civilians got killed on that day. The Defence case is that according to this witness, there is some so-called friendly gunfires which killed their own civilians and soldiers. But the Prosecution's case is that they were murdered deliberately by some people. Well, of course, there is a dispute between the parties. The question is we'll see whether this witness is the right person to comment on that videotape. However, we'll see how it goes, and we will make a ruling when the time comes on that last issue. So could we have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re, please continue with your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness J.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I just want to go back to yesterday afternoon when I was asking you about where you were on the 14th of September. Now, you gave some evidence you were there in the afternoon when soldiers returned from Uzdol. Did you remain in the communication centre throughout the day, that is from the time the soldiers left for battle and the time they returned? When I say communication centre, I mean the hut.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you remember Mr. Halilovic visiting the hut on that morning at maybe 9.30 or 10 in the morning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At least I didn't see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Halilovic in an interview he made with the Prosecution in 2001 has said that he visited the communication centre of the Prozor Independent Battalion --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, sorry I'll just stop there. I object to this being put. There is a number of reasons why. One of them is that it's a confidential document.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: We could move into private session? Is that the objection that it's confidential.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: That's the first one, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. So shall we go into the private session if you want to put on more reasons on that? Yes. Let's go into the private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: We are in open session?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Now we are in the open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: A moment ago -- just sorry, give me one moment. A moment ago, you said that the communication centre is a separate building. Do you mean a separate building to the hut that you spoke about yesterday?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Because yesterday at page 71 to 72, I asked you: "Q. Were you in the communication centre while the attack was taking place on the 14th of September?" And your answer was: "A. I'm not sure where you get this at all, that I was at the communications centre. It's a small hut, the command. Everything was there, virtually everything. So being there, you're in all of these places at the same time, in a manner of speaking." It appears to me there is a contradiction between what you said yesterday and what you're saying today. Were there in fact two separate places, a communication centre and a command centre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were some several metres apart.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Are you saying they were separate buildings? Or were they located within the same hut? Communications and command.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was one building that we called the command, which was in actual fact a hut consisting of several rooms for the forestry workers who were there. The communications centre was an auxiliary building, an outbuilding, perhaps used as a barn or something of the sort that was situated several metres away from the hut.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown Exhibit P331.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: On the screen to your left, you'll be shown a photograph in the moment, Witness J.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you recognise the command centre of the Prozor Independent Battalion in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe it's the one on the left-hand side. Although from this particular angle, it does not really resemble that building that much.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you see the communication centre you just described to us as perhaps a barn or something of the sort that was situated several metres away from the hut? Can you see that in the photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that it is at the other end of this building, this dark roof that can be seen there. From -- looking from this angle it seems like one building but actually, these are two separate facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Just so the record is clear, would you be able to mark on that, just put a large arrow pointing down to the point where you say the communications centre is.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Witness marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Just for the -- just so it's very clear afterwards when you finished your evidence could you please put the arrow from the top -- from where the trees are going down. Do you see what I mean, going like that? So that we can see exactly where you mean. We have to look at the photograph later, you see.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Witness marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you put a line down, please, in the middle, like an arrow, pointing down.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I have drawn an arrow but there you go. Is this fine now?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's good, thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: May that be received into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: It's admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P450.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you. I've finished with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you have any training or were you given any training in investigation before the 14th of September 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you know whether Erzimana Dzogic was trained in investigation or investigative techniques before the 14th of September 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I arrived a year later, so I do not know what was going on earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You mean a year after she was there, is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, roughly speaking. Perhaps a bit less than a year. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was any assistance sought from the civilian police to talk to the soldiers after the 14th of September 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I myself did not. Perhaps somebody else did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, were you aware of anyone seeking assistance from the civilian police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about the military police? Were you aware of anyone seeking assistance of the military police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The military police didn't participate in any of the statement-taking, did they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: The statements were for the most part taken by the assistant commander for security. Therefore it was the military police who was involved, the assistants for intelligence and I myself. However, I did not perceive my task as that of an investigator who was supposed to detect who the culprits were but rather to find out what had happened and to produce a report to that effect. The subsequent steps to be taken were within the competence of the security organ or the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, my question was, the military police weren't -- didn't participate in the statement-taking. That's correct, they didn't participate, did they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't claim either way. It is possible that the assistant commander for security had tasked the police officers who were under his command to obtain certain materials for him. I had no way of knowing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's because no one from the military police approached you and asked you about your statements, did they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have any specific role within the battalion in order for anyone to approach me officially.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You didn't receive any forensic assistance from either the military police or the civilian police, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: In what sense do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The normal business of forensic investigation following an alleged crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, I object to that. There is no normal business of forensic investigation following an alleged crime. If my friend has got specific things that he wants to put to the witness, he should put them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What's your understanding of the forensic process involved after an alleged crime such as a murder has been committed? What are the steps that should be taken?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, that question should be clarified. Is the question what is his understanding today or is the question what was his understanding in 1993?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And it's a very difficult question for a layman in this field. I believe the witness already testified that he has no training before he joined the army. But, however, you could try.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: To make it more specific to meet my learned colleague's suggestion, in 1993, September 1993, what was your understanding, when you were taking the statements from these potential suspected murderers, of what steps should be taken, what steps should be taken in conducting such an investigation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no instructions to that effect. I was simply told to find out everything about what had happened and to produce a report. The term that you were using just now is new to me. It is probably a very technical term, and I don't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Just so we both understand what we are saying, I'm talking about the steps that you understood should be taken in an investigation into a suspected murder in August -- sorry, September 1993.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was, and I remain a true amateur in these things. I was left to my own devices to try and find out what had happened from individual persons. I did not have any methods recommended to me or anyone's assistance in conducting an investigation. I did not really reflect that much as to what it is that I should be doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Are you saying that you didn't really consider yourself to be participating in an investigation into suspected murder of civilians in Uzdol?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what I said. I participated in the process of establishing the truth about what had happened. Whatever I could contribute with my knowledge, through conversations with people, I tried to contribute. Now, as for the rest, as for the general process, I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was anyone overseeing the work you were doing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was nothing to be overseen there. I was simply talking to people, noting down my observations, and when I thought that I had gathered enough information, I produced a report.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Between the 14th of September, that's the day of the attack, and the 20th of September, 1993, did you seek advice or assistance from any person as to what you were doing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no need for that because the assistants for security and intelligence were the ones tasked with that. I did what I thought was relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: So there was no oversight and you sought no assistance from anyone. Did anyone give you guidance as to how you should go about your task or were you just asked to go around and talk to people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not that there were no guidelines because I did talk to the two assistants and consulted them on some matters, and a conclusion was drawn as to what had to be done, the tasks were distributed, assigned, and I took charge of my tasks. But there was no need for any additional assistance. As to whether there was any control, I don't know. Perhaps what I was doing was being controlled by someone after all.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said a moment ago that you were "simply talking to people, noting down my observations, and when I thought that I had gathered enough information, I produced a report." Where did you note down your observations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had a notebook that I used. It was a rather a notepad that I carried with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What did you write in it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just brief comments after talking to soldiers and listening to what they had to say. I would simply jot down whatever I thought was important and decided to leave my further conversations with these interlocutors that I thought were important for later.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm not quite sure I understand what you mean by "leave further conversations with these interlocutors that I thought were important for later." Can you please clarify what you mean by that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: The soldiers were recounting what they had experienced. Some of them exaggerated the events in order to emphasise their role in them, and I was not interested in listening to such accounts. I wanted to come down to the main points, to listen to those who were there, who had firsthand experience about these events. And I decided not to continue my conversation with these people who had firsthand knowledge of the events in front of everybody else but rather decided to talk to them later, on their own.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Let's go to the process. When you were talking to people, were you talking to them in groups, these groups of soldiers who had been in Uzdol on the 14th of September?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes I did not even take part in the conversation. I simply listened to what they were saying. Sometimes I broached some topics in order to lead them to the areas that I was interested in. But I did not have any methods that I used consistently.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What I'm after -- what I'm asking you about is the process of speaking to people. When you were talking to the soldiers, were you having conversations or listening to them amongst groups of soldiers? Were groups of soldiers talking to you at the same time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were spontaneous conversations. They were not prepared beforehand. I took part in conversations even concerning football. But whenever the action at Uzdol came up, I took a more active part in the conversation and tried to lead the soldiers to talk about some areas I thought were very important.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: But when you were doing this, was -- you're saying it was in a group, amongst a group of soldiers talking about general things and then Uzdol would come up and you would ask them a few questions about it. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not the one putting the questions, because in that case, nobody would talk to me, in fact. I merely listened to what they had to say and tried to appear to be asking additional questions out of curiosity, rather than appear to be directly interested in what they had to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: So you wouldn't have had your notebook with you when you were talking to groups of soldiers about general conversations in which Uzdol came up? When I say you wouldn't have had your notebook out, in front of you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You made these notes later, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Straight after.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You weren't instructed -- you weren't given a list of people to speak to about their possible participation in the murder of civilians in Uzdol? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, it was us who had to establish the people to be interviewed, in the same way that I've just described for you. I was actually the one who was in charge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where were you having these general conversations with the soldiers? In what locations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, at Dobro Polje, and there was another village three or four kilometres to the south of Dobro Polje. The name of the village is Scipe.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And where in the village were you having the conversations? Was it in the open, in a building? Where?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no specific location. I knew a great many people in that village. I would sometimes go there to have coffee with someone, to have a chat, just like that, nothing special, really. Any place would have been good enough. The local playground, someone's house, the front yard, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And how many soldiers were in these groups that you were talking to or listening to when they were having general conversation in which Uzdol sometimes popped up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could have been two, three or ten, depending on the circumstances, on the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And were people talking about two, three, four, up to ten people talking about Uzdol in the same conversation, and their experience of it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Uzdol was not the only thing that was brought up in these conversations. In their spare time, people would pick mushrooms, grill mushrooms. They would just sit down, have a smoke, talk to each other. That sort of thing. So it was not very clear-cut situation where something specific was being discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When the topic of Uzdol came up, I'm just talking in general terms, was it something that the soldiers generally would start talking about and telling you of their experiences of being in Uzdol on the 14th of September?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were different groups, and whenever someone started talking about that, it would usually be like that: Where were you on that day, what happened, do you remember this or that? And then there would be these conversations between two, three, four or more people. I would just listen in and try to conclude who was where and who did what, based on their recollection. There certainly was information that I was able to glean from such conversations. Important information, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And was it from these conversations that you made your conclusions about what had happened in Uzdol on the 14th of September 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly from these conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I just want to -- I'm just waiting for something on the transcript to come up. If you would just bear with me for one moment. A few moments ago you said when talking to these people some of them would exaggerate their role in what happened in Uzdol. What sort of things were they telling you which you thought were exaggerations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for the most part, everyone -- well actually not everyone but those who tended to exaggerate would boast, trying to emphasise their own bravery, saying that they were fearless in given situations, stuff along these lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did anyone boast about how many civilians they had killed on the day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This wasn't something that I ever heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You didn't hear about them killing children? None of them mentioned that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In these conversations, did any of these soldiers mention at all killing civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No civilians, no soldiers. No one was really prone to tell stories about how they themselves had killed anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Or did they mention that anyone else had killed anyone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would leave it vague for the most part, no names were named but people were saying that all sorts of things had happened and that the situation was difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, what do you mean by the situation was difficult? What did they say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were running across the village, they feared for their lives, they no longer knew what to do. There was a lot of random shooting. They were shooting around and they were being shot at. They were throwing hand grenades. When I spoke about exaggeration, well, this is an example. Someone might have been exaggerating, talking about their own acts of bravery in what they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Witness J, you had no way of assessing whether they were exaggerating, because you weren't there; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not specifically, but I have quite some experience distinguishing truth from lies. That plus my intuition helped me to draw certain conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: But your intuition didn't tell you that some 29 civilians had been murdered in the village on that day, in all your conversations with all these up to 100 soldiers after the 14th of September 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did know that civilians had been killed, although no one told me straight out.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You knew civilians had been killed because it had been on the radio, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember whether I heard this on the radio or perhaps it was our commander who told us. Probably something was said on the radio too.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You think it was your commander, you mean Enver Buza?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I'm saying I can't remember specifically whether he told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You were aware from the first day that civilians had been killed in that village, weren't you? That's the 14th of September.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said earlier, the first time I met someone who was involved in Uzdol was at Dobro Polje, the morning of the 14th. He was very crestfallen. Being as downcast as he was, he told me that all sorts of things had been going on. So he couldn't tell me what precisely but I sensed he had a need to share this with someone. So my conclusion was there must have been civilians at stake too and that many people had been killed on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, what led you to believe that? Was it your intuition again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was based on his reaction that I concluded there must have been civilians involved. I looked at him and I could tell that he was going through a bad phase. He may have done something like that himself, although he never told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: He may have done something like what? Killed civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: He wasn't specific. That was a conclusion I drew based on how he told me. I pushed him to say what exactly had happened, who got killed and how, and then he would just reply, well, I can't talk about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said yesterday that this was being discussed over Bosnia. You said that it was -- and it was on the radio. The allegation at the time was that there had been a massacre in that village, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Hang on. Is it being put to the witness that he said there was an allegation of a massacre or is it being put that it was on the radio? There is three different propositions there and the witness has got to be able to be clear which ones he's being asked to comment on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, be specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The allegation, when these soldiers returned on the 14th of September, was that there had been a massacre in the village. That was what was being said, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the question has got to be specific.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I know. I know. Who said that? From the radio, from the soldiers? From his commander?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. I withdraw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You heard allegations from around the 14th of September that there had been a massacre in that village, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not certain when I heard this referred to as a massacre.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: But it was before the report of the 20th of September, wasn't it? That's the report that Buza signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Hang on a minute, hang on a minute, just stop. That -- Your Honours, the report that my learned friend is referring to, if it's the exhibit, it's got a date of the 20th of September on it but there is no evidence that it was a report of the 20th of September. It's just got a stamp saying it was received at that particular time. So my learned friend has to make sure that he's identifying the document properly and accurately before he puts it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, so long as the witness understands what kind of report the Prosecution referred to, I think there is no problem. Mr. Re, you may try to put your question more specifically to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: My suggestion to you is that you had heard or you knew of the allegations that there had been a massacre in Uzdol before this report, which has the date of the 20th of September on it, and Buza's name, was sent somewhere. I'm saying you knew that before this report was compiled. Didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible, but I can't commit myself. I can't specifically recall the day I first heard this described as a massacre.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about a mass killing of civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what you mean by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about the -- the killing of a number of civilians during a battle? You were aware of that allegation before that report was compiled, weren't you? Whether it's called a massacre, a mass killing or a killing. You were aware before that report was compiled that it was alleged that a number of civilians had been killed, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The footage of the aftermath of the ABiH attack on that village showing bodies of civilians was shown on Croatian TV, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about that. Didn't see it myself, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Of course, no one asked, as far as you're aware, the Croats to provide you with a video of Uzdol in the aftermath of the ABiH attack, did they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no communication at that level, at the battalion level, or with the HVO. There may have been communication going on between the top-most levels of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Certainly no one in your command, in the Prozor Independent Battalion, as far as you're aware, was provided with a copy of the footage from Croat TV, were they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You're also aware that BBC journalists or international journalists had visited Uzdol immediately or the day after the attack, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about this from some people who could actually see it happen from the elevation, with Uzdol in view. They said that some -- the vehicles belonging to an international organisation rather tried to drive into Uzdol but what people said at the time is that these vehicles were prevented from entering the village by HVO soldiers. But this is something that other people told me and not something I saw for myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The intelligence you had at the time was that an international camera crew had been into Uzdol, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Information I had was that there had been an attempt by a team to take footage in Uzdol, but they were stopped from doing that by HVO soldiers, and it wasn't until sometime later, I don't know exactly when, that they were allowed access. That was what I heard. There was no way I could check this myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And your information was also that this footage had been broadcast by the international media, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours he's just denied the proposition on which that's founded.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: He just said they were allowed access.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe the previous question is about HVO's TV footage and here it's about the broadcast by international media. Maybe that's a different angle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, it could be so, Your Honour and if it's clarified I don't object to the question about it, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said your information was then that they were allowed access. As a result of their being allowed access, you were aware, people in your command were aware that footage of Uzdol had been broadcast in the international media; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, again this is one of those questions that's double-loaded. The question should be either he was aware or people in the command was aware. So that had better be specified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. That's a reasonable objection. Mr. Re, let's go straight -- let's go step by step.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I certainly will.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: People in your command were aware that as a result of the international media being allowed access to Uzdol, footage of Uzdol had been broadcast in the international media; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew nothing at the time. We had no access to any of the media, not even the radio. There weren't enough batteries to go around.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was any attempt made to your knowledge by anyone in your command to attempt to get copies of any footage this international camera crew may have made in Uzdol when they were allowed access in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you aware of any attempt being made by anyone on the ABiH side to obtain the assistance of the authorities in Herceg-Bosna or the HVO to conduct an investigation into what had happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: This wasn't possible at the battalion level. As for higher levels, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Is it an appropriate time? We started at ten.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I'm in your hands. If you believe you are changing subjects, we could have a break. I think we'll resume at 5 to 12. It's a strange time. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yesterday, your evidence was that on the 14th of September 1993, you first came to speak to Osman Hero, that's at page 27 of the transcript, and he had a need to tell you about what will happened and after about an hour or so you entered the office where Erzimana typically worked and you found "her there taking statements from Hero and another man whose name I can't remember. I think it was Jusuf." And you asked her what was going on. "And she said well, we have to take statements. We have been asked to draft a report. And then she said, now that you're here, let's do it together. Therefore, I stayed there, taking the statements." Now, that was what you said to the Court yesterday afternoon.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: My question is about the report. Was it a combat report that she was drafting?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Your Honours, it isn't said that she was drafting a report at that time at all. It said that she was taking statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I object to this. I just read back the witness's evidence to him, "We had been asked to draft a report". My question is was she drafting a combat report. How can this possibly be objected to?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: It can be objected to. I'll explain it, Your Honour. The question confuses two things: What Erzimana Dzogic says she's been tasked to do, which was to draft a report, and what she was doing at the time when she -- when he went into that office. So if the question is related to when the witness went into that office, then in my submission, it's quite clear that she wasn't at that moment drafting a report at all but was taking statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I object. He can stop this now. He can stop putting words into the witness's mouth. This is most improper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, let's see how the witness could answer this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: My question, Witness J, is whether it was a combat report that she had been asked to draft.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No combat report of any sort. And I don't really understand what combat report means.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your evidence yesterday was, "We had been asked to draft a report. And then she said now that you're here, let's do this together." You mean by that, let's do the report together, don't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what I said. Perhaps you misunderstood me. I entered the room where Erzimana was talking to that soldier. I was listening for a while, and then she addressed me and said, well, good of you to come because we have to draft a report. I did not even ask her to clarify what sort of a report she had in mind. I merely stayed on listening to what she was doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you ever find out what sort of a report she was in the process of compiling?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably just as I did, she wanted to find out what had been going on down at Uzdol.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You're saying probably. Are you telling the Trial Chamber you never asked her what sort of report she was asking you to assist her with when she said now that you're here, let's do this together?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't discuss the report at the time at all. We were listening to what the men had to say about what had happened and we each took down notes. She did as she saw fit and I did as I saw fit.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was there any coordination between the two of you as to which task each of you were doing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes we would consult each other and exchange information, in order to let the other one know how far we had gone ahead with the information we had gathered. But it was on an informal basis where we would come across each other and simply ask whether the other had any new information.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Are you telling the Trial Chamber that you never found out what sort of report it was that she was asked to draft or was drafting or you were assisting her with drafting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that we compiled a single report based on what we had found out. So it's not that I don't know what the report was about. The report was about the events at Uzdol on that specific day, taken as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Who drafted the report? Who wrote it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that I was writing one and I do remember that there were several.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The report that she was asked to draft, who wrote that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe she did. Who else could have done it?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, a moment ago you said that now that you're here, let's do it together. When I say a moment ago, your evidence yesterday was "we had been asked to draft a report and then she said now that you're here, let's do it together." So I think you answered it yesterday when you said who else could have done it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, it's not appropriate to put arguments. My friend can put a question but not simply put two statements as he has there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think that's just what Mr. Re did. He put the statement to this witness and asked the witness to give some clarification or explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, if that's what the question is, then I've got no objection. It appeared to me that it was propositions but if I'm wrong, I'm wrong, and I don't object to any questions, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Just so it's completely clear what I'm asking you, a moment ago I asked you who wrote the report. You said, "I believe she did. Who else could have done it?" And yesterday you said, "We have been asked to draft a report, and then she said now that you're here, let's do it together." I'm asking to you comment on what you said yesterday; that is, that she suggested the two of you do it together.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: The report that was supposed to be made could not be drafted on the basis of conversation with a single soldier so the moment I entered the room, she was not drafting the report but was, rather, doing all the preparatory work for the report and she said okay we will do the report together, meaning that in one of the following days we were supposed to compile together all the different pieces of information we had gathered. So on that specific day she wasn't drafting the report. She was merely doing the preparatory work for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How did she write it? What did she use to write the report?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe she used a pencil. That was the usual practice. We didn't have any other facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The report she produced was a handwritten one; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first version, yes, definitely. Whether somebody else typed it out at a later stage, I don't know. I know how I wrote the report, and I did it by hand. Then I went to the communication centre. I dictated it out to the person who typed it out, and then sent it on to whoever he thought had to be -- had to receive the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: So can we be clear here? How many reports --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 6th Corps [interpreter's mistake].

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How many reports were there? Did you and Ms. Dzogic do separate reports?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe we did, yes. But I never saw the final version of her report. I may have seen it, but I don't remember. I believe there were at least four or five reports to the best of my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Produced by whom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that Buza wrote one report because I assisted him by providing some information I had gathered. I know that I myself produced one, Erzimana did and I suppose that Mustafa Bektas also did. He was the official assistant to the security commander. That's why I inferred that there had to be at least four.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And the report that Buza produced, are you saying it was based upon information you provided him as to what happened in Uzdol? Based upon your speaking to up to a hundred soldiers who were there on the day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He had his sources of knowledge, of information. He consulted me and made some corrections to his report, if any.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: So you dictated the report, it was typed up, and sent off to the 6th Corps.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How did Buza get a copy of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: This witness hasn't said that Buza did get a copy of it. So that question is not legitimate yet. There has to be a step taken first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said a moment ago that you assisted Buza, who wrote a report, by providing him with some information you had gathered. Did you assist him by providing him with a copy of your report?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't. We only spoke about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you tell Buza that your information was that no civilians had been killed in Uzdol?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What did you tell Buza?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did Buza obtain a copy of your report?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. He could have obtained a copy, had he wanted to, but I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The Defence counsel have provided us with a statement of your proposed evidence last week and this is what Defence counsel have told us that you told them last week. "Subsequently he," that's you, "wrote a report which Buza saw and which was sent to the 6th Corps in the normal way." That's what you told Defence counsel, isn't it? That you wrote a report and Buza saw it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible that he did see it but I do not remember the details. I did not give him the report or insist that he read it. I don't remember the details. Therefore, I can only suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, what Defence counsel have provided us with does not say subsequently you wrote a report and possibly Buza saw it. But it says, "Subsequently he," that's you, "wrote a report which Buza saw." You appreciate there is a difference, don't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see the difference, yes. But ten years later it is not possible to remember all the details. Not ten years but 12, 13 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was your information about the number of Croatian soldiers and civilians that were killed in Uzdol during the attack on the 14th of September 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember ever hearing a specific number of the soldiers and civilians killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. Without being specific, what's your -- what was your information about -- generally, about the numbers of civilians and soldiers killed on the Croat side?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first thing I heard was on the Croatian media, who had reported that there had been over 100 civilians killed. Later on, the numbers varied. I heard some figures from Buza at the command. I don't know where he got the information from. But I never heard the same figure twice. To this day I do not know what the actual number was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was your conclusion, after speaking to the soldiers, with the hundred or so you spoke to or up to a hundred or so you spoke to, about how these civilians died?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody saw a soldier or a civilian killed, except in one particular instance where the driver was captured by the soldiers and they took him to his command, forcing him to invite the others to surrender. Therefore, I never heard from -- anyone say that they had seen a person killed in order to be able to recount this. They all said that they were running across the village, seeking shelter from the shooting, there was shelling there as well. There was general confusion. Everybody was concerned with for saving their own skin. They were not able to observe clearly what was going on. They were simply trying to save their lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And was that the information you put in your written report?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Roughly, yes. Yesterday I read a report and I said that it largely corresponded to the impressions that I gained of the events.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That was the report of Mr. Jasarevic, the chief of military security, which I think you said was based, you think, upon Mr. Buza's report; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: That's too compound, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What, for the average lawyer?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I object. And it's too compound.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Let's go step by step.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When the witness was shown Mr. Jasarevic's report yesterday, he said he thought it was based on Mr. Buza's report. I'm merely putting to the witness what -- the evidence yesterday. It was Exhibit 229? 232.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In any event, Mr. Witness J, yesterday you were shown the report of Mr. Buza. Now, are you saying that that largely corresponds with the impressions you gained of the events?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't referring to that report or to Mr. Jasarevic's report. I believe there was a third report that I was looking at. I can't remember whose it was. And it was that report that I meant when I said that it largely corresponded to my report. I did not agree with some of the details, where the report stated that women were used as human shields, and I disagree with that. Therefore, I was referring to a third report that was shown to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, could I just indicate that if the witness is to be questioned about these documents, it's just a matter of fairness, he should have the specific document put on the screen in front of him so that he can recall. We all know the numbers and we call them by shorthand but if the witness is to be confronted, he has to be confronted properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I believe Mr. Re put a proposition first and depends on the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I agree and it wasn't an objection so much as a future comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Later on, I believe that if the Prosecution believe there is a need, he will put that report, if it's available, to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Exhibit D236 is probably the third one, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your help.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Witness J, the report you're referring to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Your microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The details -- okay. You said it largely corresponded to your report but you specifically disagree with the women being used as human shields. That was the point of your disagreement with that report. I'm about to show it to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown Exhibit D232?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Should that report already be on the screen in front of me?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I hope so. Could you just, please, go to page number 2, which is the body of the report. This is the report of Mr. Jasarevic. Is that the one you're referring to when you said that you agreed with the contents except the bit about the use of women as human shields?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, the learned Prosecutor knows which one he was referring to because it's in the transcript from yesterday and the document was shown to him and he made comments about it. Now, I've got no objection to the transcript from yesterday being read back. It's very difficult for the witness to say what was said yesterday in connection with a particular report unless the transcript is put -- in fact it's pointed out to me here that on -- in any event, Your Honours, the witness can answer the questions. I'm sorry, just let him answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I am putting the witness -- putting to the witness the report he discussed yesterday at page 55 to 56. That's 232. In case there is in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Just to clarify it, Witness J, is that the one you're referring to when you say you agreed with the contents in general, or generally agreed with it, but you disagree with the bit about the use of women as human shields?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that I stated that I had not seen this report and that I presumed that it had been drafted on the basis of Buza's report, but I was not referring to this report. I was shown three reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, yesterday, when questioned about this you said, page 56: "A. I see this report was based on Buza's report. After Buza's report was compiled, I helped based on such information as I had. But I don't remember some of these things being part of my original investigation or findings, such as the number of casualties or the emphasis that is placed on women with weapons. I don't remember having come across these things myself during my investigation. However, as to the fact that everyone was armed and the fact that their artillery had caused the best part of the devastation, that certainly holds true." Now, that's what you said yesterday in response to Mr. Morrissey when he asked you whether what is in this report was consistent or inconsistent with the results of your "investigation".

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Firstly, no question has been asked. Secondly --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I was waiting for the translation. That's what you do here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Secondly, there is no words quote unquote around the word investigation there. That's a quote from the Prosecutor. And if he's going to read transcript we can do without his additions, Your Honours. It's just, in my submission, not helpful -- any way that's the protest I make about the current question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe that Mr. Re, you have to make sure that this is a document the witness referred to yesterday on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There is no dispute about that. It's page 56. Mr. Morrissey was examining him on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I know. I know. It seems to me there is some confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Not in my mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: No, no. In my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: The point is to make me clear. It's not about you. So I hope you could ask a question about the document on the screen, whether there is the document the witness referred to yesterday, and later on, continue your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The question and answer I just read to you, do you remember giving that answer in response to Mr. Morrissey asking you about the document on your screen now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your questions are so general and so complex that it's very difficult for me to keep my focus up. Please try to be more specific and to the point about your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Look, I'm not trying -- please, I'm not trying to confuse you in any way. I'm just trying to work out what your response is to this document. Yesterday -- are you saying now that you're not sure whether the answer I read to you yesterday was in response to this report?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, Your Honours, look --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can I --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: No. Your Honours, that question is confusing and meaningless and I submit that it's not permissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Let's go step by step. You have to have a good basis, then build the building on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I don't know where to go. My learned friend keeps objecting. He has accused me of using the wrong document. I've put the right document to the witness. I've read back to him his answer from yesterday. I'm asking him whether he remembers the answer, the witness says it's confusing. Now, he's already given the answer that it was consistent. As a part of it I want to ask him about and about Buza's report. I keep getting objections every time I put a passage from yesterday to the witness. The last objection I don't understand. The witness said he was confused so I'm saying are you able unable to remember whether you were referring to that document? I mean, what do I do? Do I take him back and take him through everything that Mr. Morrissey asked him yesterday?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may ask him a very simple question: Is there the document you referred to yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you remember seeing this document yesterday? Do you remember Mr. Morrissey showing you this document yesterday and asking to you comment on it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say you're being imprecise there again. I saw three documents yesterday. What you're asking me about, what I can see on the screen, is not the document that I referred to when I said it was consistent with my impressions. I did speak about a number of details that I disagreed with. There is another document that I saw yesterday, I'm not sure about the number, and that was the one I refer to when I said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All I'm asking you is do you remember seeing that document yesterday. Do you remember Mr. Morrissey showing you that particular document which is on the screen now yesterday.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember this document, and I said I'd never seen it before. But I assume that it was compiled based on Buza's report. That's all I can tell you about this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Is the information there consistent or inconsistent with what you learned from your speaking to up to a hundred or so soldiers in the days or weeks after the attack on Uzdol?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is one thing I must say. Was it you who changed the document on the screen now or -- because this might lead to further confusion, in case you decide to ask me about what I can see in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I don't want to confuse you. I'll give you a paper copy which make it easier for you to read.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: My question was who changed the document on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm not guilty. You'll have to -- it's not me. I have no control over that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Is that -- is the information in that document, which is Mr. Jasarevic's special report dated the 20th September 1993 consistent or inconsistent with the information you gained from talking to up to a hundred soldiers in the days or weeks after the attack on Uzdol?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's consistent for the best part. Not entirely, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I just want you to tell the Trial Chamber which parts are inconsistent. Is it the bit about sending the -- using the women as human shields, which is in the second paragraph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's it. I never heard anything about that, women being used as a human shield, carrying weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: But otherwise, the information is consistent with what you were told?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said for the best part. I'm not sure if you want specific percentages.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I just want you to tell the Trial Chamber which parts of that are not consistent with what you were told by the soldiers you spoke to in the days and weeks after the Uzdol attack.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I've just said. I took this to mean that the HVO brought some women along to be used as a human shield and that the women were given weapons to carry. I never heard anything like that from any of the soldiers and that's why I said I couldn't agree with this. It's not consistent with the information that I had. Aside from which -- I'm also not familiar with this information here that seven wounded soldiers were evacuated and when one of those killed was being evacuated, four more were killed. I'm not familiar with how many fighters and civilians were liquidated. These were numbers that I could not ascertain myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. But it's the numbers, not the fact of the liquidation, that you're -- that you were unaware of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea how people -- where people got this number from. The only possible source that occurs to me right now is the Croatian media.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown Exhibit D149.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It will come up on the screen as well. That's the report of Mr. Buza with the date of the 20th of September 1993 on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I object to my friend adding that detail about the date being on it in that way. True, it is that it has in the top left, the handwritten date. But as to the sending of this document, it's just -- I'll withdraw the objection just now and I'll see what happens. But I just want it to be pointed out that there has been some questions about that with other witnesses, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. I think this point is in the record already. But anyway, this document bears the date, so there is no problem for the Prosecution to refer this document as the document itself. You may proceed, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's also only for the purposes of the record, so that when you read it later you know exactly which document we're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Morrissey showed you this document yesterday. Do you remember that, Witness J?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in detail, but I must have seen this one somewhere. I'm familiar with what it appears to be stating.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Now, what role did you have in the drafting of this report?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume Buza might have consulted my opinion on this, asked me whether I had anything to add. I can't remember the specific conversation that we had but that's what I assume might have happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You think that Buza may have used information you gave him to compile this report?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he may. We talked on a daily basis. Of course he would have been in a position to use my information. I never tried to conceal anything I knew from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Which information in this report do you think you gave him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult to specify. It was the overall picture that was created in a discussion that everyone was involved in. It's difficult to specify my part and his part. It's difficult to distinguish. We exchanged information. We listened to each other. Therefore it's very difficult for me to specify now which part is mine and which was based on someone else's information.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were Ms. Dzogic's conclusions about what happened in Uzdol similar to your own?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so. Not that I can necessarily remember what her impressions were. I don't think her general conclusions were any different from anybody else's.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: As far as you know, none of the soldiers she spoke to provided information to her about the killing of Croat civilians or soldiers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think some did, but I have no accurate information to show this. As far as I can remember, this person called Hero, whom I found in her office, was saying something along these lines but I can't remember the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You're saying, aren't you, that out of the up to 100 people you spoke to, not one gave you any information from which it could have been concluded, "About 65 Croatian soldiers and about 30 civilians, mostly armed, were liquidated during the operation"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: You keep referring to the specific figure. The 100 people that I allegedly interviewed. It might be a figure of speech. I might as well be saying I spoke to 200 or 300 people, as many as that, because I did talk to a great number of people. Officially and unofficially. I was there when consultations were conducted, and people were interviewed. Therefore you shouldn't take this figure of 100 persons as something that is necessarily set in stone. The impression I gleaned based on my interviews is reflected in my report. What I said is that one of these reports was roughly speaking consistent with the impression that I gleaned from my own interviews.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, is it this one?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean Buza's report?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yeah, the one in front of you. Is that the one which is roughly consistent --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. This report contains a lot of details that are familiar and that I arrived at myself, but there was a third report, another one, that I looked at. Can't remember which one it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can the witness please be shown Exhibit 227.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Is that on the screen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is no report at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, I'll be corrected if I'm wrong, but I believe those were the three reports that were shown to you yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: D236 is the other one, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I apologise. And could the witness please be shown 236.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's the report dated the 31st of October 1993, signed by Nermin Eminovic. Would it help if you gave you a paper copy?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's the one, the one that I read yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yesterday, you said that "What I felt and found at the time was quite similar. This is perhaps slightly more detailed." Are you saying that report contains more detail than you were able to gather in speaking to up to a hundred people after the 14th of September?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What I'm saying is my general impression is for the best part consistent with what this report appears to state. As for the level of consistency concerning specific details, well, I think I did say about this detail where there is reference to the bus driver, Slavko Mendes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When you said yesterday, page 56, "However, as to the fact that everyone was armed and the fact that the military -- that their artillery had caused the best part of the devastation," that certainly holds true. What was the devastation you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no way I could have established that, that the best part had been caused by artillery. I said provoked not caused but this wasn't something that I could arrive at. This was, Your Honour, the real devastation that occurs when a shell falls on an inhabited settlement or near a house.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, if there was no way of you establishing that the best part of devastation had been caused by the artillery, why did you say to the Trial Chamber yesterday, "However, as to the fact that everyone was armed and the fact that their artillery had caused the best part of the devastation, that certainly holds true"?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours before that's proceeded with I just ask the Tribunal to notice that that question that's being put to the witness related to a different document to this one and you'll see on that page that the question that my learned friend is now putting to him concerning devastation does not relate to document D236 at all and in fact, the document D236 comes the next line afterwards. We will find you the reference, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: My answer is, and so what? I'm not talking about this question. There is no question I'm talking about that document. I've finished with that document. I've moved on. Why is there an objection in the middle of my question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Because it didn't appear that my learned friend had moved on. He left the witness with the impression that we were still on that one. I'm sure he didn't do it deliberately, but perhaps it had better be made clear that he's moved. Then I won't object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. I believe the situation is clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Now, after -- I'll have to take you back to the question I asked you. And I asked you if there was no way of establishing the best part of devastation had been caused by the artillery, why did you say to the Trial Chamber yesterday, "However, as to the fact that everyone was armed and the fact that their artillery had caused the best part of the devastation, that certainly holds true"? The question is why did you say that if you had no way of establishing it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were able to glean a lot based on the testimonies of soldiers who witnessed the destruction. Furthermore, we could watch this from a hilltop near Uzdol. That was BH army controlled. It was easy to see what sort of devastation occurred. Not in great detail but you were able to get a general picture. Besides, I don't remember I spoke about the best part specifically. That would have been a very random choice of phrasing. This would have been something to be established in a thoroughgoing investigation. If I used the phrase, it was by accident.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: So are you now withdrawing what you said yesterday, that you could no longer tell the Trial Chamber that, "The fact that their artillery had caused the best part of the devastation, that holds true"? Are you now withdrawing your evidence to the Trial Chamber yesterday?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm not withdrawing my evidence. I'm simply saying that this particular word or, rather, expression, "for the best part" does not hold. What I wish to state is that I believe that most of the destruction was caused by artillery. Now, to what extent, I cannot talk about the nuances. I was merely talking in logical terms, that it must have been artillery that caused the best part of the devastation. It could not have been caused by infantry weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What are you referring to, devastation? Do you mean the deaths of civilians and soldiers, or what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: When there is shelling, the artillery is used to target homes, facilities, and not persons. The HVO artillery was falling throughout the village. Now, what they were targeting is something that I cannot claim with any certainty. One can only speculate.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You're sighing as far as you're concerned, HVO shelling caused the deaths of 29 civilians in Uzdol on the 14th of September 1993. That's the devastation you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's a highly improper question. He can ask whether that's what the witness is saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I just did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: He can ask the witness to clarify. He cannot tell him what he said. And my submission, given the answer it's repetitive on other answers. But in any event, I won't object to it if it's phrased as a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re. Maybe you could rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Are you saying that your conclusion was that HVO shelling caused the deaths of the civilians who died in Uzdol on the 14th of September 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: In part, of course, yes. It was caused by shelling. But nowhere did I claim that only shelling was the cause of death of civilians. They perished because they were in the midst of a conflict between the HVO and the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: So some were shot in the crossfire and some were killed by shelling; is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I object to that. It's irrelevant for this witness to now say what happened. What is relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Why did you lead the evidence yesterday?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Morrissey, I see no problem with this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: As the Court pleases.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: So is your evidence that some were shot in the crossfire and some were killed by shelling?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours, could I just renew that? Your Honours, the issue is -- it's not an objection to the form of the question.
