It's just this: That this witness is not a crime-scene person and the Defence is not calling him as a crime-scene person. We are calling him concerning list own knowledge at the time and why he did what he did and so on. I don't object to my learned friend asking was that his belief then. The objection is to ask now in a general way what -- as to this -- for this witness to ask -- to answer what happened. So I won't object to it if it's put to the time when it actually occurred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think the precondition for this question is that based on his interview, his talk, with the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Witness J, some were caught in the crossfire and some were shelled?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your evidence over the last two days has been that not one of the up to 100 people you spoke to told you about any deaths of civilians. On what basis could you possibly draw a conclusion as to how any of them died or the fact that any of them died?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never claimed to have established how many were killed, but the conclusion could easily be drawn from the different accounts I heard. I could infer what had happened from what I heard in these stories. I did not hear anyone say that they themselves participated in the killing of any civilians, but when taking all the stories together, one could draw inferences.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: If people have not told you about civilian deaths or that any civilians died, how could you possibly draw an inference that they had died and how they had died?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on what the soldiers who took part in the action said, and based on the picture that I formed. They were saying that they were running across the village, there were hand grenades that they were throwing, they were being shot at. In addition to that, one could hear on the media how many civilians and soldiers were killed. I cannot tell you with precision when it was that I created this clear picture of the events, but whoever was talking about these events described them as having been terrible. And I heard many different stories only as a passive listener and by actively talking to these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: But you've told us in not one of those tellings of different stories were the deaths of civilians mentioned.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, because nobody wanted to say out in open that they were the ones who had killed any civilians. I heard stories from others. One of the first persons I talked to about it left me with an impression that he had done something that was against his moral beliefs and my conclusion was that probably he was shooting at a house or throwing a hand grenade at a house where there were civilians, not only soldiers. He himself felt the urge to talk to me about it. I could see that he was having a hard time. And my impression was that the reason behind it must have been the fact that one of the civilians got killed. He probably would not have had such a hard time had a soldier been killed, because there was a war on after all. That's why I concluded that it must have been a civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: But because he didn't tell you, it was mere speculation on your part, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think anyone would admit at the time to having killed a civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said that you heard stories from others. Who were the others you heard the stories from and what were these stories?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Roughly the ones that I mentioned already. They were telling me in which direction they were running, whether they were throwing hand grenades at houses or whether they were seeking shelter or being exposed to fire. And I would in passing also ask them about the killings, and everybody's reply was that they had not themselves participated in the killing, but I did infer that there were killings involved. However, nobody would name any names. Perhaps it was difficult to even know who the person shooting at civilians was or perhaps they knew but simply would not talk about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Everyone's reply was that they had not themselves participated in the killings, but you did infer there were killings involved. Yet you just told us that a large part of the devastation was caused by HVO shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, can I say I want to object to this. I submit that this is now becoming argumentative and repetitive. My friend can ask questions about any specific he wants but we've now reached a point where in my submission this is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We have spent a lot of time on those questions. I believe that the point is very clear. I don't think it's necessary to continue on this subject, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And is it the case that no one, of all the people you spoke to, told you that any civilian deaths were caused by HVO shellings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was difficult for anyone to claim anything to that effect. How could one know whether a person perished due to shelling, hand grenade or gunfire? I don't believe it likely that the persons could have perished from gunfire, given the intense shelling that was going on at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said you could see the shelling from the hill overlooking Uzdol. You weren't up there, were you?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, he didn't say you could see the shelling. He said you could see the devastation. In my submission, that's a distinct difference in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Let me check the transcript. My recollection is different. I'll just check it. The witness referred to devastation caused by the artillery, that's at page 54, and then said we were able to -- "Furthermore, we could watch this from a hilltop near Uzdol. That was BH army controlled. It was easy to see what sort of devastation occurred." So I pressed the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I don't mind it being pressed. I just want the right -- the evidence to be put back accurately to the witness before it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: If there any difference between artillery and shelling, I don't know what it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, there might be some difference between devastation and shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You just spoke about intense shelling. Was that the sort of thing you say you might have been able to see if you had been on the hilltop overlooking Uzdol?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me first explain this bit where you talk about us being able to follow what was going on. There must have been an error in interpretation. There is a difference between when you say that you can see something and you can follow something because it -- what I meant to say was that if we wanted to, we could see the devastation from the hilltop, and of course whoever was on the hilltop at the time could also observe shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The question is just you weren't up there, were you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't, not at the time of the fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You didn't see any of this devastation with your own eyes, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: The time when the devastation was inflicted, no, but I could see the consequences of shelling from the hilltop.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was a statement taken from --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Sorry, could I just intervene one moment, Your Honours. We just detected something might have been missing with the interpretation. Mr. Cengic tells me that the witness mentioned the word binoculars which wasn't translated. Could it just be clarified with the interpreters whether that's the fact or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the witness use that term.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Maybe, Mr. Re, you could ask the an a question on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When you said you could see the consequences of shelling from the hilltop, did you just say a moment ago that you could do that with binoculars?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you take a statement from (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't, but I was present there when he was talking about his experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When was that? And where was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was at Dobro Polje, several days later. I can't remember exactly. He was a member of the command and I saw him on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What did he tell you about his experience about what had happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing special. The only thing that remained in my memory was that he had set out with only one round of ammunition, and I memorised this bit because I found it ridiculous that somebody would just go out into a battle with a pistol.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did Erzimana Dzogic take a statement from him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you see the statement she took?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Just a second. How can my learned friend -- well, I won't make a speech. I object to that. He says he doesn't know. The next question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I quite understand. It's not logical to ask a second question. If he knows --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I said statements. I wasn't referring to that witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm not talking about that witness. He said no. I've moved on. I said did you see the statements she took. I'm talking about other people. But to make it clear --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Maybe you have to specify your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you see the statements - that's with an S on the end - any statements that Ms. Erzimana Dzogic took from anyone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't customary for me to take her statements and vice versa. We could have exchanged information on some matters but I do not recall the two of us actually exchanging anything of the sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How did you take your statements? What did you physically do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean the method of work or the premises where it was taking place?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Both. Just tell me what you did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I object to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Not again!

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: This is repetitive and Your Honours, in my submission, we went over this, the method in which these statements were taken before. If there is something specific I don't object to it, but the general questions once again are repetitive and it becomes oppressive, in my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. I believe so. The witness has already answered that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I haven't asked him anything about taking statements. At all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: The witness testified before that he has a notebook and he took the statements -- on that notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. With respect, that's not correct. That was when he was talking to soldiers in groups. I haven't asked him anything at all about his taking of statements. That was when he took notes when he spoke to groups of soldiers and he did that afterwards. I haven't touched upon the statement-taking process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, if there is a difference between notes and statements, you may continue with your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You understand what I'm talking about? I'm talking about your statements, not the general notes you took when you spoke to groups of soldiers.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. How did you take the statements from the soldiers? What was the process you employed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already stated that I would jot down a few lines and the names of the persons who I found interesting, and then I would tell them to drop by whenever they could, to have a chat. We would go to the office that we used as the premises for security and intelligence-related activities, and then I tried to find out more about some of the pieces of information provided by the person or the names and so on, to form a clear picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And did you put this same -- this information in the same notebook that you were using to make your notes of the conversations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I had a different notebook that I used for writing down the statements in their proper form, with the date, the name of the person taking the statement, that is mine, and the name of the person giving the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you using -- I think you said pencil before. Were you handwriting these? I'm sorry, of course you were.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were these ever dictated and typed up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How many of them were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember, but quite a few.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you give an approximate number? More than ten, less than ten? Less than five? More than 20? Less than 20? Whatever.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had other statements in the same notebook that had to do with other issues related to the battalion. There were 50 or 60 sheets in all that had been used up. And of these, some 20 pages could have been used up in relation to Uzdol but I'm talking in rough terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What did you do with the statements when you finished taking them in this book?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used a metal filing cabinet that we had in the corridor where we kept all the documents related to our activities, and I kept it, the notebook, there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did the people you took the statements from sign these statements? Did you ask them to sign them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When you were taking the statements, you weren't investigating allegations of murder in Uzdol, were you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I understood was that my role was to investigate as thoroughly as possible what had been going on at Uzdol and who had been involved, and then, based on that, to draw up a report.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's not what I'm asking you. I'm asking you whether you were investigating murder in Uzdol, and you weren't asked to investigate possible murders in Uzdol, were you?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I just -- it has to be clear what the proposition is that he's being asked to comment upon. The question was asked and answered. If my friend has a different question to ask, it should be detached from the previous one. It may be there is a different question being asked but it has to be clear what it is and in my submission at the moment it's not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Maybe the possible what had been going on at Uzdol, including murder.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: My question, and this is deliberate. Every time I get somewhere, I get these objections. My question is deliberate. It's as to what he was specifically investigating, whether he was investigating an allegation of murder. It wasn't answered. Now, that objection was completely unfounded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: In my view, the witness answered partly of your question but the problem is that you have to make some specification or clarification on the answer given by this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Witness J, you were not investigating allegations of murder in Uzdol on the 14th of September 1993 when you were speaking to the soldiers, were you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand my role to be that of a murder investigator. This would have been impossible to do with Uzdol. Had I been meant to conduct an investigation like that, I would have needed to know precisely who the victims had been or who the perpetrators had been. However, this was not what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And it wasn't what Erzimana Dzogic was doing either, was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe she could possibly have had more information than I had. We didn't know who specifically had been murdered, nor how many, nor where exactly it happened, nor who the perpetrators had been.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: As far as you know, there was no investigation going on at the time into an allegation of murder of civilians in Uzdol on the 14th of September 1993, was there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No, but I'm suggesting to you, as far as you know, there was no murder investigation or no investigation into murders in Uzdol going on at the time, was there?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I object to this. The witness has made quite clear what he understood his own terms of reference to be and what his own job was as he understood it to be. It's not for him to characterise this investigation one way or other. That is the job for you, the Tribunal, to do at the end of the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I allow Mr. Re to continue with his question because the answer given by this witness is not clear. He answered no, I didn't say that. What does it mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: As the Court pleases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, so Mr. Re, has a follow-up question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What I'm suggesting to you is that as far as you knew, there was no investigation into murders in Uzdol on the 14th of September 1993, going on when you were talking to the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what I was doing at the time then. I was investigating the truth because that was part of my investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Not what you were doing, but what others were doing. As far as you were aware, no other people were investigating murder in Uzdol on that day, were they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, both Erzimana and Mustafa Bektas were carrying out investigation. Officially they were assistant commanders. I don't know who else should have been involved at the battalion level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Re, at this point, could I ask you how long do you still need to finish your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Not too long. Probably about half an hour, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, in this case, I believe that I made a mistake for us to start an hour later this morning. Well, I think the tapes are running out because we have been sitting here over 90 minutes already, so we have to stop now, and we will resume at 3.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.37 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. Before we start, Mr. Morrissey, you have something to read?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm sorry. I'm sorry to do it and I'm sorry to revisit old ground, but at the time -- this morning we raised an issue with you about a statement or part of a statement of a particular person. I think we should go into the private session for me to raise this matter now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And it is our intention to finish the testimony of this witness in one sitting. And tomorrow, we would like to have another witness. We'll start from 9.00 until we finish the testimony of that witness, because we will be very reluctant to have this witness to spend the weekend in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It appears to me that that witness will finish quite quickly so there is every likelihood we will finish him in the morning session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Before the break, I was asking you, Witness J, about (redacted). You said he was on the command and you were in daily contact with him. I'm just saying that to refresh your memory about what you said.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I say something before I start answering questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Is it connected with the question I'm asking you or is it connected to something else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that the Trial Chamber is aware of the fact that I have certain health issues, despite of which I still decided to come here. Therefore, I would kindly ask you to keep your questions very brief because it is difficult for me to maintain concentration necessary to answer long questions. Especially since I'm expecting results of my medical tests, which are due tomorrow, and this is something looming on my mind. Additionally, I have another cause for concern which is related to something that the Prosecutor asked me yesterday, namely he asked me whether I was charged by the HVO for rebellion. I said yes, that was right, there was an indictment of the then-illegal HVO concerning some alleged rebellion. However, that was not so important for me because none of those charges were substantiated. They had no witnesses, no evidence, despite the fact that they tried hard to find them. So this kangaroo court, if I can call it that, was -- its proceedings were annulled and the matter was never mentioned after 1992. What does concern me, however, is that this information, obtained by the Prosecutor, regardless of how discreet they were when looking for this information is something that jeopardised my security, because I believe that since the matter is not recorded in any documents, this information could only have been provided to the Prosecutor by the former archives of the security services of the then HVO. Therefore, I reiterate: Regardless of how discreet they were when seeking this information concerning me, this has certainly put the spotlight on me and thus jeopardised my security, because those who provided this information about me can certainly understand that I'm being discussed as a potential indictee or something else. I wanted to inform the Trial Chamber about this because I did not expect this type of outcome in the course of my testimony. I believed that the protective measures granted to me ought to have protected me against this. That's all I had to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, thank you very much for your statement. On the part of this Bench, I can guarantee you that we will do everything to protect your security. As for the procedure on the part of the Prosecution, I believe they have kind of set procedure taking full consideration of the security of the person they are looking for. So I don't think at this stage there is any problems on that. If you found something which is -- might affect your security, you may inform the Tribunal or inform the party calling you to be a witness. As for the first point, I would like to say that I've already got the confirmation from the parties that we will try to let you go as early as possible, taking into consideration of your health conditions. I believe that we will finish your testimony before 4.30. Yes, Mr. Weiner?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, just to clarify and to let the witness feel assured, when we go after and seize archives or obtain archives, we seize them or obtain them in very large numbers with regard to documents in the thousands if not tens of thousands and we've had in the hundreds of thousands at a time. We are not going to the security and saying, here is a name, give us that information. This is part of a seizure which was -- where documents were taken in large numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well, Witness, are you ready to continue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am, with the proviso that I have to contradict what we just heard. This document could not be located in any archives. Therefore, it could not have been seized together with a large number of other documents. However, I believe that I said sufficiently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. If you are not at ease, I may ask the Prosecution to talk to you on this very subject after you finished your testimony. Yes, Mr. Re, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I won't be long. I'm almost there, Witness J, and I'll try and keep my questions very, very short for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I was asking you about (redacted). Now, (redacted), as a part of the command of the Prozor Independent Battalion, was in a position to know whether an investigation into the events in Uzdol was being conducted, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's right, since he was assistant commander for, I believe, morale or something along those lines. I'm not sure what it was called.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Now, in -- he gave evidence here and on the 7th of April, at page 70 of the transcript, he was asked: "A. Now, Witness, do you know whether any investigations were conducted into the civilian deaths in Uzdol?" To which he answered: "A. I'm not aware of any investigations and I don't think I ever said anything about any investigations. This is not something that I am familiar with." Now, all I'm going to say to you is, you don't have any reason to disagree with what he said, do you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have no reasons, although I am surprised.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: But you would accept that he is in a -- he was in a better position than you to know whether investigations were being carried out because of his position on the command -- as assistant commander for religion and morale, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, look, I object to that. It's just -- this witness has given evidence about what he did and this question is frankly I put this proposition: That is an absurd question to put. It's not acceptable to put that question here when this witness has given evidence and been cross-examined on the basis of the inquiries that he himself made. I remind the Chamber, my learned friend in putting that proposition there, I remind the Chamber of what it was that (redacted) said that that he was doing in those days. I don't have the transcript at fingertips but I can well remember what it was in general terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I really object to my learned friend, in front of the witness, saying that. The witness has given his evidence about his daily contact with (redacted). So if he wants to make the objection, it should be taken in the absence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe that the Prosecution asked a very tricky question. But, however, we'll hear what the witness is going to tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: As the Court please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that he was in a better position because I myself was constantly present at the command headquarters. I was in contact with Mustafa and Erzimana, whereas he was mostly out in field. In addition to that, he originates from a village from that area. This is where he was from. So he frequently went home, whereas I remained at the headquarters and could hear everything that was going on. I was better informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yesterday you spoke about -- you told the Trial Chamber -- could we just move into private session for one moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We will go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Witness J, I just want to ask you about something that you spoke about yesterday. Mr. Morrissey asked you about your information about Uzdol, and you told the Trial Chamber that -- about your information, about who was living there, and you said "We also knew that each house had at least one barrel," that is one weapon, "sometimes more. What we were positive about is that each house in the village was armed." Now, that -- I'm just putting -- I'm just reminding you of what you said yesterday. I'm going to ask you a question. That is, you agree, fairly specific information you say you had about the contents of every house, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And are you confident of that information that there was a long barreled weapon in every house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm almost certain because the army and the HVO were a single formation from the beginning of the war, that is April 1992, until October 1992, in Prozor, and even longer in some other areas. We had contact and we knew what they had and they knew what we had, and also, the purchase of weapons was no secret. Weapons were being sold in the streets. We knew who was buying weapons, who was distributing weapons, and where. So even little children had all this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Is what you're saying that you knew specifically that there was a weapon in every house in Uzdol, or is that a guess based on the fact the HVO had been there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know on the basis of some facts. There was a joint action by the army and the HVO against facilities of the former JNA, where a large amount of weapons were seized and then these weapons were distributed in proportion to the number of inhabitants between the Bosniaks and the Croats. Apart from this, the Croats had an organised service to collect funds for the purchase of weapons and all those who were working abroad were obliged to send money to that fund, and we knew approximately how many weapons were purchased, when, and where they went. That was no secret.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What I'm getting to, though, is the fact that they were in every house as opposed to the village. Did you have specific information that there was a weapon in every house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm almost certain. Of course I wasn't able to check this but I was convinced that every house had weapons. That's what people said. Not just one weapon but more than one. People even boasted about the number of weapons they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And of course, knowing that there were weapons in every house you would have known who or exactly who was living in each house in Uzdol, in September 1993, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see what that has to do with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, you just told us you had precise information that there were weapons in every single house. I'm suggesting if your information is that precise, you would also have known the identity of all the people living in Uzdol in September 1993.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have to know that. I saw my neighbours and among them were some from Uzdol, who carried weapons openly. Nobody concealed their weapons from anyone. Maybe I was speaking figuratively when I said every house, although I'm convinced that it was actually every house, but nobody collected information about who was living in what house.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And because nobody collected that information, as of 14th of September 1993, you wouldn't have known how many civilians were still in the village, would you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see any connection between those two things. We couldn't even know who was a civilian and who was not. I'm referring only to men, of course. Of course, children were civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Are you telling the Trial Chamber that as of the day of the attack, you, from your position on the Prozor Independent Battalion, did not know the identity of the women, children and civilians living in Uzdol, and where they lived?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew some of those people from an earlier period, but people from neighbouring villages knew each other individually. I was just a foreigner in those parts, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's not what I'm asking you. I'm asking you about whether from your position on the Prozor Independent Battalion you knew the identity and where people lived in Uzdol, civilians specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, in fact the question was originally, women, children and civilians, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Witness J?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you please repeat your question in precise terms and briefly?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What I'm asking you is: Did you know, on the 14th of September 1993, the identity of women, children, civilians and where they were living in Uzdol?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean all the inhabitants of the village?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Women, children and civilians, yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a ridiculous question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, you told the Trial Chamber yesterday and today you believed every house had a weapon in it. I'm asking you -- I withdraw that. That's a very precise piece of information you've given the Trial Chamber. I'm asking you -- you're saying the precision of your information didn't extend to the identity of the people living in those houses where those weapons were kept?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me something I don't understand. Are you asking me whether we had a list of people living in each individual house and what weapons they had, details of that sort? I don't know what you're asking me about.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's a start. Did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is there a list? Is that what you mean? We were not a Registrar's office, nor was it possible for me to draw up such a list. We had general information about who was in the village, where they were, and what artillery they had, what weapons, infantry weapons and so on, and approximately how many women and children were there. But only approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you have information on where the women and children were living? Which houses they were living in? What parts of the village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to our information, women and children were mostly in Prozor, some ten kilometres away from Uzdol. But some of them would go there when they thought it was safe because they had land there and they probably went to harvest and so on, work on their land. But no women or children lived there on a permanent basis, either in our villages or their villages in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you have information on the location, that is where these weapons, long-barrelled weapons, were stored, in each of the houses in Uzdol?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stored in houses? Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, yes. You've told us that every house had a weapon. Did you have any information as to where these weapons were stored in each of these every houses that had these weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every one who came home carried a weapon and they would put their rifle down next to the door when they came in. That's what happened there. There weren't any warehouses as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And before the soldiers went into battle in Uzdol on the early -- in the early hours of the morning of the 14th of September, were they instructed to go looking for these weapons in these houses in Uzdol?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't present when they were given their last instructions, but I know that they did have some kind of talks. I don't know what their instructions were but I don't believe it was to look for weapons. In such a situation, they wouldn't even have time to get to the houses. As far as I was able to understand, they simply ran through the village. They didn't even have time to look around.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: (redacted) I'll ask you about Erzimana Dzogic. From her position in the command of the Prozor Independent Battalion, she was in a better position than you to know whether or not an investigation was being conducted into the events in Uzdol, wasn't she?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe she knew more than I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: She gave a statement to the Prosecutor on the 20th of May 2001, and in that statement, in the very last paragraph, she said, "I do not know anything about any offensive operation conducted by our battalion in the village -- Croatian village of Uzdol." Now, that's very different to what you've told the Trial Chamber yesterday and today, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had I known what it would have cost me, I would probably also have said that I knew nothing. She probably knew enough to say that she didn't know anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: She was then interviewed again on the 22nd of May 2003, and gave a signed statement to the Prosecution, and at paragraph 22 of the statement, she said, "From a civilian, I heard Rama Radio broadcast about the killing of some Croats that had happened in Uzdol. I received the information with disbelief because Rama Radio had broadcast information before which proved to be wrong. I thought of it more as propaganda. What I heard at the time from the conversation between a civilian from some other village and the villages of Scipe was that some people from Uzdol got killed. I did not take it seriously because Rama Radio was propagating and was under the control of HVO, such as some people were announced to be dead and I would later see them in the street while I was still in Prozor. I do not know those who they are any more." Now, listen to this line, which finishes it: "As much as I remember, there was no comment made by soldiers about that event to me." Okay? You've heard what she said to the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I object to that, Your Honours, "you've heard what she said to the Prosecutor." My learned friend is not entitled to put that she said that to the Prosecutor. He's entitled to put that he's got a signed statement in his hand which says that. He can't put that she said that at all. He can put what the statement says, not what she said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I see there is no great difference between the two expressions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: As the Court pleases.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Having heard the quote I just read to you, what she -- the statement -- what she said in the statement she signed is very different to the evidence you've given about what she was doing, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, I object to that comment. Your Honours, that last sentence which my learned friend focuses on says, "As much as I remember there was no comment made by soldiers about that event to me." And when you look at what was talked about in the lines before, there is discussion of "Rama Radio propagating and being under the control of the HVO such as some people were announced to be dead and I would later see them in the street while I was still in Prozor." Now, my submission, it's not open to my friend to say that that line there is very different because it's simply a matter of interpretation what that line is referring to. He can ask the witness -- since Your Honours have allowed that to be put, he can ask the witness for his response but he can't -- Mr. Re can't put his own interpretation or gloss on that line, if my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. I believe there is some reason in the objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In my submission, it's own capable of two possible interpretations. One is that Mr. Dzogic is referring to what was broadcast over Radio Rama, which is that there was a killing of civilians, and the other one is that they had actually done it. So it leads to the same point. The evidence of the witness is that she was taking statements from witnesses as to what happened. Now, the statement can be read in two ways, but it comes to exactly the same point. It's that no soldier made any comments to her about what was broadcast on Radio Rama, what which is about the killing of civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: In this paragraph, we did not see anything about taking statements from the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No, but Witness J has said she was speaking to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I know that. So I don't know what's the point there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'll approach it another way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Soldiers who were giving statements to -- I withdraw that. You said you saw Ms. Dzogic taking a statement from Hero and another man whose name you can't remember but you think it was Jusuf. That's on page 27. And you said you stayed there taking statements. Now, these statements were about what happened in Uzdol, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And in these people, that's Jusuf and Hero, giving information to Ms. Dzogic, they were making a comment about what had happened in Uzdol, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who made a comment?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The soldiers she was talking to when taking statements, they were making comment to her about what had happened in Uzdol, weren't they? Because that's why she was asking them questions.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: This refers to one man, Hero. His first name is Jusuf. I saw him with Erzimana and she was talking to him and I stayed to listen.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was she talking to him about Uzdol?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And was he making comment to her about what had happened in Uzdol?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was telling her what he had decided to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: So if she said in a statement that, "As much as I remember there was no comment made by soldiers about that event to me," that's different to what you're telling the Trial Chamber, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I object to that again. Your Honours, this witness is not making any comment about Erzimana Dzogic's memory at all. Now, what you have in your hand here or what's been put is that when this witness, assuming that she said this, said "As much as I remember there was no comment made by the soldiers about that event to me," it's not appropriate to ask -- to put to this witness that that's inconsistent with what he says. All Ms. Dzogic says, if that's her talking, is as much as she remembers. You can't ask this witness to comment on her memory and I now renew the objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. I agree with the Defence counsel on the objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said to -- earlier today I asked you about Croatian television and a broadcast of the footage from Uzdol. And -- this is at page 31 of today. I asked you about the -- about that and you said, "I heard about that but I didn't see it myself, though." Now, did Enver Buza talk to you about the broadcast on Croatian TV of bodies in Uzdol?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember having talked with anyone about that broadcast. I just heard that there had been a broadcast. I didn't see it and I didn't feel the need to discuss it with anyone especially.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did anyone say to you that the footage broadcast on Croatian television was a clumsy editing job?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did hear that there had been some details there that did not fit in, that weren't really -- didn't fit in with what had been shown.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you remember who you heard that from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't remember that. It sticks in my memory that someone said that some things there had been set up.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Halilovic, when he gave an interview to the Prosecution, this is at page 19 of tape 24, 1, said -- there is no names mentioned in this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You can try.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: He said, "I saw even on Croatian television of Herceg Bosna some footage of what had happened in Uzdol. At my next meeting with Enver Buza I asked him if he had seen the footage because I insisted with Enver Buza, commander of the 6th Corps, to verify" -- sorry -- "and the commander of the 6th Corps to verify whether there were any activities that are not permitted and should they return in that there should be such activity that legal actions should be taken. Enver Buza repeated that no activities that are not permitted had taken place, that this happened at all, and he also said that the footage that was broadcast on Croatian television was actually a clumsy editing job that was done by Smjrko Sgold [phoen] because in the background one could see on the footage planes, flatlands, and the area in question is flatlands." Sorry: "Is not in the flatlands, is in the hilly regions and one can also see in the footage traces of snow and at that time there was no snow there."

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, it's not open to just read out slabs of an interview. If there is a question arising out of it the question should be asked. I object to any more of this, frankly. I won't object to this question if there is a question that comes after it. Looking at that there, there could be no -- I won't make a speech. I object at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I haven't asked the question yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I believe Mr. Re is setting up the background. The question will be followed very soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: For my friend's benefit, I do actually pause to allow the interpreters to finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Now, Witness J, having heard what I just read to you, does that refresh your recollection as to whether or not Mr. Buza was the person who told you or mentioned that there was a -- that there was something wrong with the footage on Croatian TV?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I object to that. How can it refresh his memory to read out somebody else's record of interview? You can refresh his memory from something he said or a statement he made in the past. So I object to that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That doesn't accord with the jurisprudence of the Tribunal and I specifically refer Your Honours to the Hadzihasanovic case. You can refresh recollection from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Different cases are different situations. I believe that you tried it again, then you put something to refresh the memory of this witness. But how could this witness's memory be refreshed by the conversation with others?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The Hadzihasanovic decision is an appeal decision which says that recollection isn't -- refreshing isn't confined to a witness's own past statement. It could be from anything relevant. I'm putting to the witness something that has been said by -- to relevant period contemporaneously. He said he heard something similar. He didn't remember whether it was from Buza so I'm asking having heard that does this refresh his memory as to whether it was Buza who said that. He can say yes, no, or it doesn't assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think different cases have different situations. I believe that you have already asked this question to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What I want to suggest to you, Witness J, is that what was actually happening in the Prozor Independent Battalion from the time the soldiers arrived back on the 14th, was that a cover-up was going on as to what actually happened in Uzdol that day.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not how I saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Halilovic, when he was interviewed by the Prosecution on the -- in 2001, at page 17 of tape 11 part 2, was asked: "Let me ask you this: Do you believe that Enver Buza knew that something had happened?" He responded, "A. I think he did. "Q. And Suljevic? "A. I'm not certain about that. As for Buza, as far as Buza is concerned, I'm 100 per cent sure that he knew because Buza had in his unit security officer, a security officer who of course has his associates amongst the troops and although he may not have found out about it on that very day but very soon after that he would have known. He then again had a platoon of military police. So as far as he is concerned, I'm absolutely certain that he knew about it, that he covered, tried to cover up the crime. I'm also certain about the chain of command from that battalion towards the 6th Corps. I'm completely certain that the commander and the security corps of the officer of the 6th Corps knew and of course Jasarevic was also informed about that." Now, what Mr. Halilovic said to the Prosecutor there is entirely correct about the cover-up, isn't it? Because that's exactly what was going on. Buza knew and was attempting to cover up the crime.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand why this is being claimed, because I don't agree with this. I don't agree that this was considered a crime and that it was covered up. I adhere by that today as well. I don't see it as a crime. I don't agree with how it was portrayed in the media and now in this indictment. In my mind, this has always been a military action in which unfortunately the civilians were caught in crossfire while the soldiers were trying to extricate themselves and flee from the village. I don't see how somebody has the right to qualify this as a crime. I'm making a comment about the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any redirect?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I have no questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Judge El Mahdi, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Witness, I wish to thank you for coming to this Tribunal. I have two clarifications which I would like to ask from you. The first has to do with what you said concerning the orders received by your battalion. You said you didn't remember the orders, the other orders, except those which came from the 6th Corps. Do you remember having received other orders concerning investigations on the events of Uzdol -- in Uzdol?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember receiving a written order to conduct investigations. Rather, I was told this orally. Perhaps the commander had a written order but I don't remember seeing it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But were you told whose order it was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose that the order came from the 6th Corps, because that was the typical procedure. They would forward all orders to the battalion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Thank you very much. My second question would be a clarification about what you said concerning the relations between Mr. Halilovic and Mr. Buza, Enver Buza. You said that their relationships were tense between those two, and you also said that the battalion was not well organised, was disorganised, and you added that Mr. Halilovic didn't enjoy much appreciation among the officers. Could you tell us a little more on this score, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know Mr. Halilovic. I only saw him on television. I also didn't have much information about Enver Buza. I only met him upon arriving at Dobro Polje. However in their mutual contact between Mr. Halilovic and Mr. Buza, I was able to see that they had known each other from before and that there was a certain animosity between them. What surprised me was that the commander of the battalion, which was a small formation, was able to talk to the commander in such a manner. At the time I believed Sefer Halilovic to be the commander of the army. Therefore, it surprised me that a commander of a battalion would dare to have that attitude towards his commander. In addition to that, I was able to observe certain officers who displayed quite a similar attitude. There was an officer called Mujizenovic [phoen], I don't know exactly what his position was but it was definitely well below the position of Mr. Halilovic, and judging by his attitude, I was able to see that he did not have anywhere near sufficient amount of respect that one would expect of an officer towards his commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, you conclude that Mr. Halilovic didn't have the clout necessary for this battalion? Or influence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: My impression was that he had no practical power at all. At one point in time, I saw that a part of the brigade came to Dobro Polje and then decided to go back on their own without checking with anybody. That disappointed me quite a great deal. I realised that this was not a proper army, that there was no order there or subordination. I'm not sure whether this is the correct military term.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A last point on which I would like to have clarification is about the person you met and who seemed troubled by the events, and you said this person needed to communicate this information to someone. Do you remember by what he had been troubled, disturbed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was immediately after the Uzdol operation. It could have been nine or ten in the morning. I can't remember now when this person came. He was pale, tired, looked badly. I asked him what had happened and he just waved with his hand and said, "Don't ask me. All kinds of things happened." I tried to get the details and he spoke to me in general terms. He said, "A lot of us got killed. We were really beaten. But we also did some things that I can't really tell you about." That was the gist of what he said. He was quite distressed at the time so his words were not coherent and focused. He was probably troubled by the memories about what had happened. My impression was that he was going to faint. That's how bad he looked. Perhaps this was all caused by fatigue and fear. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. And what I'm interested by is what they have committed or he has himself committed. Did you get the impression that either he or some members of his unit had committed some actions which disturbed him, shocked him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that he was in that condition because he himself had shot or had thrown a grenade. I remember some bits that he said. He said, "We launched grenades, fled, jumped over fences," and so on. Based on that, I concluded that he either fired in an area where he knew there were civilians or he threw a grenade there, or did something else that he wasn't supposed to do. He didn't tell me that in those exact words but that was my conclusion. I could see that he could not forgive himself for what had happened. That means that something was troubling him deeply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge El Mahdi. Any questions out of Judge El Mahdi's question?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you, there is one matter from the last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That relates to that incident.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I said that he had told me about throwing a grenade on a house. What he said to me was in general terms. He said that there was firing, that grenades were being launched, that he did that too. Now, as to the effect that produced, I don't know. I don't remember any further details. I don't remember him saying, "I threw a grenade on to that house and that there was somebody in that house." It would be ludicrous to expect me to remember such details after 12 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I don't think I can clarify the two parts of the transcript. They speak for themselves, in my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Mr. Morrissey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Nothing, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Just for clarification for the witness, those documents were obtained from the HVO archives which are part of the state archives of Croatia. They were obtained the 27th of April 2004 which is approximately 14 months before this person ever became a witness. So for the record, these were obtained over 14 months ago. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think I instruct you to talk this to the witness after our sitting. Yes, Mr. Morrissey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, that matter that was raised earlier on, was actually raised in private session yesterday. It started off not in private session but then I asked for it to go in private session. So I ask that it be appropriately redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll check with the previous transcript to see whether we should have it redacted or not. Thank you for telling us about that. At this stage, are there any documents to tender on the part of the Defence? No? And on the part of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, unless you want those two statements marked for identification. I can certainly have them provided to the Registry later. I'm in your hands. I don't plan to tender them but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: If you don't want to have them tendered, so there is no need for us to give a number to it. Unless in the future you are going to use it again. I'm not sure. Well, Witness, thank you very much indeed for coming to The Hague to give your evidence. I understand that you are in poor health condition and I'm very sorry for your testimony, which took so long. But, however, after we adjourn, Madam Usher will show you out of this room and we wish you a good health as well as a very pleasant journey back home. Thank you very much, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, the hearing for today is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
